layers.name: Active pharmaceutical ingredient (API)
layers.role: The component that produces the therapeutic effect.
layers.why: It is the reason the tablet exists. Its dose, solubility, stability and particle properties shape every other choice.

layers.name: Diluent (filler)
layers.role: Adds bulk so a very small dose can be made into a tablet that is practical to handle.
layers.why: Many drugs are needed in milligram amounts, which is too little to compress on its own.
layers.examples: Lactose, microcrystalline cellulose, starch, dibasic calcium phosphate.

layers.name: Binder
layers.role: Holds particles together so the compressed tablet has mechanical strength.
layers.why: Without enough binder, tablets can crumble or cap.
layers.examples: Povidone, hydroxypropyl methylcellulose, starch paste, pregelatinised starch.

layers.name: Disintegrant
layers.role: Helps the tablet break apart in fluid so the drug can dissolve.
layers.why: A tablet that does not break up may release drug too slowly.
layers.examples: Croscarmellose sodium, sodium starch glycolate, crospovidone.

layers.name: Lubricant (and glidant)
layers.role: Reduces friction between tablet and die during ejection; a glidant improves powder flow.
layers.why: Prevents sticking and helps consistent filling, though too much can weaken tablets and slow dissolution.
layers.examples: Magnesium stearate, stearic acid; colloidal silicon dioxide as a glidant.

layers.name: Coating (optional)
layers.role: A thin film for appearance, taste masking, protection, or to control where and when the drug is released.
layers.why: It can protect the drug from acid, mask a bad taste or ease swallowing.
layers.examples: Film-forming polymers with plasticisers and colourants.

systems.name: Immediate release
systems.principle: Designed to disintegrate and release the drug soon after administration.
systems.how: Uses disintegrants and soluble excipients so the tablet breaks up and the drug dissolves promptly.
systems.good: Simple and widely used; effect is not intentionally delayed or prolonged.
systems.limits: Plasma levels can rise and fall, and dosing may need to be more frequent for drugs with short half-lives.

systems.name: Sustained (extended) release
systems.principle: Designed to release the drug slowly over an extended period.
systems.how: Uses a matrix or a rate-controlling coating that limits the release rate, such as swellable polymer matrices or coated pellets.
systems.good: Can reduce dosing frequency and smooth fluctuation in plasma levels for suitable drugs.
systems.limits: Not suitable for every drug. Tablets must not be crushed or chewed unless the label allows it, because this can release the dose too quickly.

systems.name: Enteric release (gastro-resistant)
systems.principle: Designed to resist stomach acid and release the drug in the higher pH of the intestine.
systems.how: Uses a coating polymer that stays intact at low pH and dissolves at higher pH.
systems.good: Protects acid-labile drugs, and can protect the stomach from irritating drugs.
systems.limits: Release timing depends on gastric emptying, which varies. Enteric-coated tablets should not be crushed.
systems.examples: Some acid-labile drugs are formulated this way.
